title: Uniform and exponential
objectives: Use the uniform and exponential distributions, and meet memorylessness.
Derive the uniform variance and the exponential survival function.

screens.title: No moment favoured
screens.prose: Your resting order will fill at some moment in the next 10 seconds. No moment is more likely than any other, so the density is flat.
screens.question: What is the chance the fill comes between 2 and 5 seconds?

widget.label: Chance of a fill between 2 and 5 seconds

hints.text: The total area is 1 and the curve is flat. How tall must it be?
The flat top sits at height $\tfrac{1}{10}$ over a width of 10.
The shaded strip has width 3 and height $\tfrac{1}{10}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the height from total area 1, then the shaded area.

byKey.width: 3 is the width of the window. Multiply by the height, $\tfrac{1}{10}$, to get an area.
byKey.half: 0.5 is the chance of a fill in the first 5 seconds. The window starts at 2, not 0.

explain.text: Area 1 over a width of 10 forces the height to be $\tfrac{1}{10}$. The window from 2 to 5 is a strip of width 3, so its chance is $\tfrac{3}{10}$. On a flat density, chance is just the share of the width.

screens.title: Wider means lower
screens.prose: This flat density on $[a, b]$ is the **uniform** distribution, $U(a, b)$. Here $a = 0$. Slide $b$ and watch the height.
screens.question: Set $b = 20$. What is the height of the density now?

options.why: With height 1 over a width of 20 the area would be 20. The area must stay 1.
You used the width as the height. The height is 1 divided by the width.
That was the height when $b = 10$. Doubling the width halves the height.

hints.text: Area is width times height, and it must be 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the area at 1: height times width equals 1.

explain.text: The area stays 1 however wide the interval, so the height is $\tfrac{1}{b - a}$. At $b = 20$ that is $\tfrac{1}{20}$. Every window of the same width has the same chance.

screens.title: The spread of a uniform
screens.prose: The mean of $U(a, b)$ is the midpoint $\tfrac{a + b}{2}$, by symmetry. For the variance, start with $U(0, w)$, density $\tfrac{1}{w}$ on $[0, w]$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $E[X] = \int_0^w x \cdot \tfrac{1}{w}\,dx = \tfrac{w}{2}$, the mean as $\int x f(x)\,dx$
On $[a, b]$, $w = b - a$ and a shift leaves spread alone, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \tfrac{(b - a)^2}{12}$

hints.text: The shortcut formula needs two ingredients. Find them first.
$E[X]$ and $E[X^2]$ come before the variance line.
Mean, second moment, shortcut, simplify, then move to $[a, b]$.

feedback.correct: Two moments, the shortcut, then the shift to $[a, b]$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $E[X]$ and $E[X^2]$ before using them.

byKey.short: The shortcut uses $E[X^2]$ and $E[X]$, so both must come first.
byKey.shift: Moving to $[a, b]$ is the last step, once the $U(0, w)$ answer is known.
byKey.twelve: Simplifying to $\tfrac{w^2}{12}$ needs the line with $\tfrac{w^2}{3} - \tfrac{w^2}{4}$ before it.

explain.text: $\tfrac{w^2}{3} - \tfrac{w^2}{4} = \tfrac{4w^2 - 3w^2}{12} = \tfrac{w^2}{12}$. For the fill window $U(0, 10)$ that is $\tfrac{100}{12} \approx 8.33$, an sd of about 2.89 seconds.

screens.title: Waiting for the next trade
screens.prose: Trades arrive independently of each other at a steady average rate of $\lambda$ per minute. The wait $T$ for the next one has density $f(t) = \lambda e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t \ge 0$: the **exponential** distribution. The shaded tail is $P(T \ge 1)$. Slide $\lambda$.
screens.question: Set $\lambda = 2$. What is $P(T > 1)$, the chance of waiting over a minute?

hints.text: Move the slider to 2.0 and read the shaded tail.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $\lambda$ to 2.0 and read the shaded area.

byKey.complement: 0.8647 is the chance a trade comes within the minute. We want a wait longer than a minute.
byKey.lam-one: 0.3679 is the tail when $\lambda = 1$. Slide to 2.

explain.text: At 2 trades a minute, a gap of over a minute has chance 0.1353, which is $e^{-2}$. Raising $\lambda$ squeezes the curve towards 0 and thins the tail. The next screen shows where $e^{-2}$ comes from.

screens.title: The tail in one line
screens.prose: Keep $\lambda = 2$. The tail beyond $t$ is $P(T > t) = \int_t^{\infty} 2e^{-2s}\,ds$, an improper integral.
screens.question: Write $P(T > t)$ as a function of $t$.

feedback.correct: $P(T > t) = e^{-2t}$. Check: $t = 0.7$ gives $0.2466$, as shown.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate the density from $t$ to infinity.

byKey.cdf: That is $P(T \le t)$, the area to the left. We want the tail to the right.
byKey.density: That is the density, the height at $t$. The tail is the area beyond $t$.

explain.text: $\left[-e^{-2s}\right]_t^{\infty} = 0 + e^{-2t}$. In general $P(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t}$, the **survival function**, and the CDF is $1 - e^{-\lambda t}$. At $t = 1$ this gives the $e^{-2}$ you read.

screens.title: Longer than average
screens.prose: At 2 trades a minute the mean wait is $E[T] = \tfrac{1}{\lambda} = \tfrac12$ minute, 30 seconds. (Integrate $t \cdot 2e^{-2t}$ by parts to check.)
screens.question: What is the chance the next gap is longer than its mean, 30 seconds?

options.why: You treated the mean as the middle. The long right tail pulls the mean above the median, so less than half the area lies beyond it.
That is the chance the gap is shorter than 30 seconds.
That is the chance of a gap over a full minute, twice the mean.

hints.text: Use $P(T > t) = e^{-2t}$ with $t$ in minutes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $t = 0.5$ into $P(T > t) = e^{-2t}$.

byKey.half: You treated the mean as the middle. The long right tail pulls the mean above the median, so less than half the area lies beyond it.

explain.text: $P(T > \tfrac1\lambda) = e^{-1} \approx 0.3679$ for every $\lambda$. Most gaps are short; a few long ones pull the mean up. The median wait solves $e^{-2t} = \tfrac12$: $t = \tfrac{\ln 2}{2}$ minute, about 21 seconds.

screens.title: Is a trade overdue?
screens.prose: Still 2 trades a minute. No trade has come for a full minute, and a colleague says one must be due any second.
screens.question: What is $P(T > 1.5 \mid T > 1)$, the chance of waiting at least 30 more seconds?

options.why: That is $P(T > 1.5)$ from the start. Given the minute has passed, divide by $P(T > 1)$.

options.text: Less than 0.3679, as a trade is overdue
options.why: You assumed a long wait makes a trade more imminent. The arrivals have no memory of the wait so far.
That is $P(T > 1)$, the minute you already waited through.

hints.text: Write the conditional probability as a ratio.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac{e^{-3}}{e^{-2}} = e^{-1}$, the same as for a fresh wait.

byKey.due: You assumed a long wait makes a trade more imminent. The ratio $\tfrac{e^{-3}}{e^{-2}} = e^{-1}$ says the odds are unchanged.

explain.text: $\tfrac{e^{-3}}{e^{-2}} = e^{-1} \approx 0.3679$, exactly the chance a fresh wait passes 30 seconds. The minute already spent changed nothing. No trade is ever overdue.

screens.title: No memory
screens.prose: The wait ahead did not depend on the wait behind. This is **memorylessness**. The geometric distribution has it for whole trials; the exponential is its continuous twin. Prove $P(T > s + t \mid T > s) = P(T > t)$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the proof in order.

lines.text: $P(T > s + t \mid T > s) = \dfrac{P(T > s + t \text{ and } T > s)}{P(T > s)}$, by the definition of conditional probability
$= \dfrac{P(T > s + t)}{P(T > s)}$, since waiting past $s + t$ already means waiting past $s$
$= \dfrac{e^{-\lambda(s + t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}}$, by the survival function
$= e^{-\lambda t} = P(T > t)$, since $e^{-\lambda s}$ cancels

hints.text: Start from the definition of $P(A \mid B)$.
Simplify the event “both” before using any formula.
Definition, simplify the event, survival function, cancel.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The definition comes first and the cancellation last.

byKey.both: Simplifying the joint event needs the definition line first.
byKey.surv: Use $e^{-\lambda t}$ only after the ratio has single events top and bottom.
byKey.cancel: The cancellation needs both exponentials written out.

explain.text: The factor $e^{-\lambda s}$ for the wait already spent cancels top and bottom. So the remaining wait has the same distribution as a fresh one. The geometric does the same for trials: past failures do not bring a success closer.

screens.title: Two densities
screens.prose: Uniform on $[a, b]$: $$f(x) = \tfrac{1}{b - a},\quad E[X] = \tfrac{a + b}{2},\quad \operatorname{Var}(X) = \tfrac{(b - a)^2}{12}.$$ Exponential with rate $\lambda$: $$P(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t},\quad E[T] = \tfrac{1}{\lambda}.$$ In a Poisson process at rate $\lambda$, the gaps between events are exponential with rate $\lambda$.
screens.question: Quotes update as a Poisson process at 3 a second. What is the mean gap between updates?

options.why: You used the rate as the mean. 3 a second means short gaps: $\tfrac{1}{3}$ second on average.
$e^{-3}$ is $P(T > 1)$, a chance, not a time.

hints.text: The gaps are exponential. Which rate?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The mean of an exponential is $\tfrac{1}{\lambda}$.

explain.text: Gaps in a Poisson process at rate 3 are exponential with $\lambda = 3$, so the mean gap is $\tfrac13$ second. More events per second means shorter waits.

screens.title: Time to default
screens.prose: A credit desk gives an issuer a constant hazard rate of 2% a year. Its time to default $T$ is in years. So $T$ is exponential with $\lambda = 0.02$.
screens.question: What is the chance the issuer survives 5 years, $P(T > 5)$? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Use the survival function $P(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $\lambda = 0.02$ and $t = 5$ into $e^{-\lambda t}$.

byKey.linear: You subtracted 2% five times. The hazard acts on whoever is still alive, so survival decays as $e^{-0.1}$, not $1 - 0.1$.
byKey.annual: $0.98^5$ treats default as a once-a-year coin toss. A constant hazard acts continuously: $e^{-0.1}$.
byKey.default: 0.0952 is the chance of default within 5 years. We want survival.

explain.text: $P(T > 5) = e^{-0.1} \approx 0.9048$, so the 5-year default chance is about 9.5%. The hazard rate is the exponential's $\lambda$: the default rate per year for an issuer still alive, close to a yearly chance when it is small. Memorylessness means a 5-year-old survivor faces the same 2% hazard.

screens.title: A fill inside the spread
screens.prose: A model says your fill lands within 4p of the mid-price, either side, and says nothing more. Knowing only the range, a common default is the uniform: it favours no price. Measure the fill from the mid, in pence.
screens.question: What is the standard deviation of the fill, in pence? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: The fill is $U(-4, 4)$. What is $b - a$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the variance $\tfrac{(b - a)^2}{12}$, then take its square root.

byKey.variance: 5.33 is the variance. The sd is its square root.
byKey.no-square: You divided the width by 12. The variance squares the width first: $\tfrac{8^2}{12}$.
byKey.half-width: 4p is the largest possible miss, not the typical one. The sd is smaller.

explain.text: Width $b - a = 8$, so the variance is $\tfrac{64}{12} \approx 5.33$ and the sd is about 2.31 pence. The uniform is the maximum-entropy density on an interval: it adds least beyond the range. It is a modelling default, not a fact about fills, so check it against data when you can.

ideas: Uniform on $[a, b]$: height $\tfrac{1}{b - a}$, mean $\tfrac{a + b}{2}$, variance $\tfrac{(b - a)^2}{12}$. It is the usual default when you know only the range.
Exponential with rate $\lambda$: $P(T > t) = e^{-\lambda t}$ and $E[T] = \tfrac{1}{\lambda}$. It is the wait between events of a Poisson process.
The exponential is memoryless: $P(T > s + t \mid T > s) = P(T > t)$. A long wait does not make the next event due.

formula.name: Exponential survival
formula.note: The continuous twin of the geometric.

summary.trap: $P(T > E[T])$ is $e^{-1} \approx 0.37$, not $\tfrac12$: the mean sits above the median. And no event is ever overdue.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\tfrac{(b - a)^2}{12}$ with $b - a = 4$.

byKey.no-square: You divided the width by 12. Square it first: $\tfrac{4^2}{12}$.
byKey.mean: 1 is the mean, the midpoint of $[-1, 3]$. The variance measures spread.

explain.text: The width is $3 - (-1) = 4$, so $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \tfrac{16}{12} = \tfrac43$. The sd is about 1.15.

quiz.prose: Large orders reach a dealer independently at a steady rate, 0.25 a day on average.
quiz.question: What is the chance of 8 days or more with no large order?

widget.label: Chance of a gap of at least 8 days

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The gap is exponential with $\lambda = 0.25$: use $e^{-\lambda t}$.

byKey.cdf: 0.8647 is the chance an order arrives within 8 days.
byKey.rate-time: 2 is $\lambda t$, the exponent. The chance is $e^{-2}$.

explain.text: The gap is exponential with $\lambda = 0.25$ a day, so $P(T \ge 8) = e^{-2} \approx 0.1353$. The mean gap is 4 days.

quiz.prose: A server's time to failure is exponential with mean 5 years. It has run for 3 years without failing.
quiz.question: What is its expected remaining life?

options.why: You subtracted the 3 years used. A memoryless lifetime starts afresh at every moment.

options.text: Under 2 years, as it is wearing out
options.why: That assumes ageing. An exponential lifetime has a constant hazard, so nothing wears out.

feedback.correct: Memoryless: the remaining life is again exponential with mean 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what memorylessness says about time already passed.

explain.text: $P(T > 3 + t \mid T > 3) = P(T > t)$, so the remaining life is exponential with mean 5 years again. Real hardware ages, which is why the exponential is a model of constant hazard, not of wear.

quiz.prose: Trades arrive independently at a steady 2 a minute, so gaps are exponential with mean 30 seconds.
quiz.question: What is the median gap?

options.why: 30 seconds is the mean. Half the gaps are shorter than the median, and the long tail lifts the mean above it.
You halved the mean. The median solves $e^{-2t} = \tfrac12$.

explain.text: $e^{-2t} = \tfrac12$ gives $t = \tfrac{\ln 2}{2} \approx 0.347$ minute, about 20.8 seconds. The median is $\ln 2 \approx 0.69$ times the mean for every exponential.
